chapter_theme: In the last ilampakam a teacher tells the king how rare it is to win a human birth, a good land, a good family, a sound body and the faultless way, and how death may cut it off at any stage; then he describes the torments of hell that the deeds of the careless ripen into.

cast.role: the teaching ascetic who describes the rarity of birth and the hells to the king (the speaker is not named in these verses)
the hero, now an old king, to whom the teaching is addressed

2749.reading: A human birth is rarer than a pole drifting in the northern sea chancing into the yoke-hole of a log from the southern sea; to escape the great wombs and gain the human state is hard.
2749.nuance: The sermon opens a run of verses (2749-2753) that each name one more thing that must also be won, so the rarity is built up by addition.

claims.claim: of all the wombs, a human birth is hardest to gain

2750.reading: Even among men, to leave behind the hunters' hill-holds and robber outposts, where one cannot even speak of water, and to reach a watered and fertile land is hard.
2750.nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard; the reading takes the first two lines as the wild hill-country the birth must avoid.

claims.claim: to be born in a good, settled land is hard to gain

2751.reading: Leaving behind the low births of hunters who kill beasts and fishermen of the sea, with their vile callings, the king is told that to be born into a good ancient family is hard.
2751.nuance: The verse treats a birth in a hunting or fishing family as lower because of its killing trade, an ethic of non-killing carried into a ranking of birth.

claims.claim: birth in a good family is hard to gain after escaping the low callings of killing

2752.reading: A body free of the diseases that pour on one like rain on dark clouds, and unspoiled by the fire of the womb, is also hard to gain.

claims.claim: a sound and perfect body is hard to gain

2753.reading: Even with the beauty of Kama and knowledge besides, to avoid the fearful paths of the four states and to hold, without fault, to the way of the Jina's teaching is hardest of all, king of the white umbrella.
2753.nuance: 'வாமன்' is read as the Jina; the 'four states' (நாற்கதி) are the four courses of rebirth (hell, beast, man, god).

claims.claim: faultless conduct in the Jina's way, avoiding the four states of rebirth, is hardest to attain

2754.reading: Even when a birth is so hard to win, the child may die in the womb like a bubble when the seed mixes like gold and silver; if it does not, it may live once the clot has set like butter.
2754.nuance: The verse and the next four trace the dangers that wait for the child before and after birth, so the chance of a full life is made smaller still.

claims.claim: a life may end in the womb before birth

2755.reading: The clot may take a tortoise shape and slip; if it does not, it appears with a full-moon form and fortune, yet may still collapse while kin weep.
2755.nuance: The last line's கண்ணனார் is hard; read here as the kin or watchers who weep.

claims.claim: even a child formed whole may be lost

2756.reading: One who gives treasure to beggars and wins a great name may still fall like a lotus in a flawless pond that has grown and withered, and perish with his kin in tears.

claims.claim: fame and giving do not guard a man from death

2757.reading: If there is no early death, one may master learning, be wondered at by women as Kama, praised for his gifts and beauty, and yet die as he goes his way.

claims.claim: learning, beauty and generosity do not save one from death

2758.reading: Many who join women in gold girdles and anklets in pleasure that has no thought of the end are cut down by Death, and the living beat their faces and weep.
2758.event: Death cuts down men in the midst of pleasure while their kin beat their faces and weep.

claims.claim: pleasure without thought of the end is cut off by Death

2759.reading: Those who bathe in the breasts of garlanded women, pass their days with their dear children, and are then struck by disease like a tiger become corpses, like those whose ship is broken in the roaring sea.
2759.nuance: The last words are hard; the ship-wreck simile is clear.

claims.claim: household pleasures end in death by sickness as suddenly as a wreck at sea

2760.reading: The verse speaks to a king who has beaten fierce foes about a slow ebbing, in which desire passes, memory shrinks, and the speaker is silent as the mute.
2760.nuance: The whole verse is hard and its connection to the sermon is not clear; the reading is a guess from a few words.

2761.reading: A request is made to the king with the tilaka and white umbrella: tell us the towns and names of the other great kings, the wheel-lords who conquered the gods' enemies and others who rose higher.
2761.nuance: The speaker and the asker are not named; the verse reads as a request that precedes the teaching of 2762 on, but this is a guess.
2761.event: Someone asks the king to name the towns and names of the great ruling kings of the past.

2762.reading: The teacher says that those who do evil sow their deeds in the field called the soul and eat the harvest, and tells the rich king to hear a little of their pain, which makes the heart shiver even to think of.
2762.nuance: The farming image (sow, ripen, eat) is the verse's own; it makes the karma a crop, not a punishment handed down by a judge.
2762.event: The teacher begins to describe the hell that evil deeds ripen into.

claims.claim: evil deeds sown in the soul are eaten later as suffering
hell's suffering is great beyond telling

2763.reading: Driven by the ripening of their deeds, they run, and sorrow falls on them like sweet fruits dropping from the palm's crown, a poison whose fault cannot be borne.
2763.nuance: Line 1 with the 'drive' of ஊழ்வினை puts the cause in the deed, with no jailer named; the verse's palm-fruit simile is hard in lines 2-3.

claims.claim: old deeds drive the soul into suffering

2764.reading: Hell-beings rise boiling and fall on a ground planted in rows with spears, lances, swords and fire-tipped daggers, and lie scattered in all directions, those without restraint.
2764.nuance: No jailer is named; the hell-beings rise and fall by their own surge.
2764.event: Hell-beings rise and fall onto a field of fixed blades.

claims.claim: those without restraint fall into a hell of blades

2765.reading: Through the burning of their disease they are tossed up like the balls women play with, burst, melt, fall back and lie wasted, says the teacher to the elephant-king of burning anger.
2765.nuance: 'Elephant-king' is the address; line 1's cooked-flesh detail is hard.
2765.event: Hell-beings bounce up and fall again in their own burning.

claims.claim: hell's suffering falls on those whose own anger and deeds earned it

2766.reading: They are hauled on a tall, iron-spiked silk-cotton tree, fire is lit below, they are put on stakes, and cut apart hair by hair, as they once pained living beings.
2766.nuance: Here tormentors (the plurals மடுப்பர், ஏற்றி) act; the verse names them only as 'they'.
2766.event: Hell-beings are impaled on a spiked tree, burned and cut hair by hair.

claims.claim: the hell-beings suffer as they made living beings suffer

2767.reading: Red dogs with drum-like voices and gaping mouths, bound by chains, bite with diamond-needle teeth; the victims cry out, but though they die they do not die, for those who hunted beasts.
2767.event: Hell-dogs tear at those who hunted, who do not die.

claims.claim: hunters are made to suffer as the hunted did, without the release of death

2768.reading: Those who ate the flesh of fish are told to come, and melted metal is held in tongs and thrust into their mouths; they cannot bear it, run, are pierced by needles in the soles and are caught in nets like deer.
2768.event: Fish-eaters are forced to swallow molten metal and are driven into nets.

claims.claim: flesh-eating is punished in hell by being made to swallow molten metal

2769.reading: The man who took another's wife, despising his own wedded love, is made in hell to embrace a red-hot copper image of a woman and cry out, as the teacher tells the elephant-king.
2769.nuance: The phrase 'ஏதிலான் தார நம்பி' means a man who trusted another's wife as easy to take; the poem makes the former pleasure return as the torment.
2769.event: An adulterer in hell embraces a glowing copper woman.

claims.claim: adultery is punished by the burning embrace of a red-hot image

2770.reading: Those who killed beasts with the bow, or took fish with nets, as the Death of living things, are thrown daily into a seething froth of fire by the tormentors, o king of the fierce spear.
2770.event: Killers of beasts and fish are cast into a boiling froth in hell.

claims.claim: those who kill beasts and fish for sport or trade are tormented in hell daily

2771.reading: The tormentors, with thick sticks, pound the hell-beings in anger, roast them in a black pan, thrust daggers into their eyes, and drive stakes through their hearts and split them like palms.
2771.event: Hell-beings are pounded, roasted and impaled.

claims.claim: hell punishes with violence that has no end

2772.reading: Unable to move their tongues for thirst, they look longingly at water, enter a lotus-covered pool to drink, and find the water turned to pus, and cry out in pain like a stand of cut palms.
2772.nuance: The word 'pasi' is used for the longing, the verse itself names thirst.
2772.event: Thirsty hell-beings go to drink in a pool and the water turns to pus.

claims.claim: hell mocks desire with water that turns to pus

2773.reading: As the hell-beings approach a canopy hung with fragrant garlands that drips perfumed water, it surges like fire fed with ghee and burns them, as they cry in pain.
2773.event: A pleasant-seeming canopy flares up and burns hell-beings who come near.

claims.claim: what seems pleasant in hell becomes a burning

links.note: In 377 the poet laments that the nectar that ends birth is rarely won and yet men pamper the senses; in 2749 the teacher shows the rarity itself, a human birth as unlikely as a drifting pole finding a yoke-hole in the sea.
links.teaches: The earlier complaint is given its measure here, so a reader sees that wasting the human birth is wasting a one-in-a-sea chance.

links.note: Naladiyar 34 tells one who has this rare body to take its full fruit, as juice from cane; 2749 gives the odds that make the body rare, the pole in the yoke-hole.
links.teaches: The quatrain's advice to use the body gets a reason in the epic's image of how improbable it is, and the epic's image gets a use to put it to.

gains.a: the verse's picture of chance gains the plain duty the rarity implies, to use the body's fruit
gains.b: the quatrain's word 'rare' gains a concrete measure, with a drifting pole and an unlikely yoke-hole in place of the bare word

links.note: Kural 338 says body and life part like a bird leaving its nest; 2754 says the life may be lost even before it leaves the womb, as a bubble bursts.
links.teaches: The Kural's picture begins at the nest-leaving; the epic starts earlier, with the embryo itself already at risk, so the loss is not only a late one.

gains.a: the verse's tale of the embryo gains the bird-and-nest image of parting that gives the loss its shape
gains.b: the couplet's parting of body and life gains an earlier start, in the womb, so the risk is shown to begin at conception

links.note: Naladiyar 25 says the man who sees kin wailing at a corpse and yet marries and expects joy is answered by the funeral drum; 2758 shows men in the heart of pleasure cut off by Death while the living beat their faces.
links.teaches: The quatrain shows the lesson refused, the epic shows the death that teaches it, and together the reader sees that pleasure and mourning are the same scene seen at different times.

gains.a: the verse's death in pleasure gains the quatrain's voice of the one who watches and still does not learn
gains.b: the quatrain gains the verse's scene of pleasure at its height, with the jewelled women and their anklets, so the cost of ignoring the drum is made concrete

links.note: Naladiyar 33 sets the fool who sighs when the fruit of past deeds arrives against the wise who accept it; 2762 says the evildoer sows deeds in the soul and eats their harvest.
links.teaches: The quatrain names the response to the fruit, the epic names how the fruit is formed, so karma is shown as both cause and the way to meet it.

gains.a: the verse's farming image of sowing and eating gains the quatrain's wise way of facing the harvest, which the hell scenes never show
gains.b: the quatrain's 'fruit of past deeds' gains the hell-sermon's scale, which shows how severe that fruit can be

links.note: Tirumular says the subtle body eats the fruit in heaven and hell and then takes another body with the old deeds following; 2762 says the evildoer eats the harvest of deeds sown in the soul.
links.teaches: Both let the deeds ripen as an experience of hell, but the Saiva verse carries the sufferer on into a new birth by a subtle body, which the Jain verse does not say here.

gains.a: the verse's farming image of deeds gains the Saiva account of what survives to carry the deeds, the subtle body
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse gains a vivid account of what 'eating the fruit' means, in the hell scenes that follow

links.note: In 347 Vijayai's distress comes because a deed of a former birth stood waiting; in 2763 the same ripening is told of all who do evil, with fruits dropping from the palm.
links.teaches: The single case of the queen's fate and the general teaching that deeds come to fruit are placed side by side, so the reader sees the sermon as the rule behind a plot he already saw.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 198 has Death's servants bind and drive the killers into fire-mouthed hell; in 2764 the hell-beings rise and fall on the blades with no jailer named.
links.teaches: The Saiva verse puts Yama's servants in charge, while the Jain verse leaves the pain to the deeds and the place, so the two show different views of who runs hell.

gains.a: the verse's hell gains the contrast of a judge's servants at work, which brings out its own lack of any
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse gains a hell without servants as a rival picture, in which the ground itself does the work

links.note: Siddhar 16 hopes to avoid being called a sinner and falling into the barren hell, by knowing the breath-thread; 2766 shows what that fall would be, the stake and the fire.
links.teaches: The Siddhar's wish to avoid hell gains a picture of what he flees, and the epic's picture of hell gets a way out the Siddhar names, knowledge of the breath rather than the Jain sermon's virtue.

gains.a: the verse's torture gains a different way to avoid it, by a yogic knowing, in place of conduct
gains.b: the Siddhar's hope gains a precise picture of the hell, so the escape is not a vague wish

links.note: Naladiyar 84 asks the adulterer what pleasure he had, since the act brings disgrace, a cut leg and long hell; 2769 sets the adulterer in hell with a glowing copper woman in his arms.
links.teaches: The quatrain names the price of the act and the epic shows the price paid, so the pleasure is seen turning into the pain it earned.

gains.a: the verse's embrace gains the quatrain's question about what pleasure was gained, which turns the scene into an argument
gains.b: the quatrain's phrase 'long hell' gains a specific image, the copper woman

links.note: Kural 255 says that if one eats flesh hell does not open its mouth; 2770 shows the killers of beasts and fish thrown daily into a seething pit.
links.teaches: The couplet says that hell waits, and the epic shows what its mouth holds, so the reader sees the rule enforced by the pain of the killer, not by a judge's word.

gains.a: the verse's hell for killers gains the couplet's plain rule that eating flesh is itself the reason
gains.b: the couplet's 'hell' gains the epic's concrete view of the pit that waits for killers

links.note: 2764 shows hell-beings rising and falling on blades; 2770 shows that the same beings are tormented daily by others who throw them in a boiling pit.
links.teaches: The sermon moves from the bare place of hell to those who work in it, so a reader sees that hell has both a ground that hurts and agents who add to the hurt.

source_issues: Verses 2754, 2757, 2758, 2763-2771 and 2773 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2760 and 2761 are hard and their speaker and connection to the sermon are not clear; both are marked uncertain.
The sermon's speaker is not named in these verses; the cast id 'muni' is a placeholder for the teaching ascetic taken from the chapter's place in the closing ilampakam.
2755 line 4 கண்ணனார் and 2759 lines 3-4 are hard readings.
